edges.description: Loss of DNMT3B-dependent methylation at D4Z4 is one route into the shared chromatin-relaxation node, alongside repeat contraction and the other chromatin-modifier loci.

The permissive polyadenylation signal acts at the transcript, not at the chromatin: it converts derepression of the array into a stable DUX4 message in muscle. Without it, derepression alone does not yield accumulating DUX4.
Loss of repression at the FSHD locus permits aberrant DUX4 expression in differentiated skeletal muscle.
Severe early-onset FSHD with large 4q35 deletions can include sensorineural hearing loss through extra-muscular intermediates not represented in the skeletal-muscle pathograph.
Retinal vasculopathy travels with the same large-deletion, early-onset end of the D4Z4 contraction spectrum as hearing loss, so it is placed here alongside it rather than downstream of myofiber loss.
Recurrent DUX4-mediated injury drives chronic muscle degeneration with incomplete repair and replacement by fat and fibrous tissue.

edges.description: Reducing Dnmt3b on an FSHD-sized D4Z4 background did not raise DUX4 transcript in skeletal muscle and produced no muscle pathology, so this model does not reproduce the node it was built to test.
edges.limitations: The transgene is a 2.5-unit human array in mouse chromatin rather than a normal-length array with a human permissive 4qA subtelomere, so the digenic combination modelled is not the human one; the Dnmt3b allele is an exon-skipping hypomorph rather than one of the patient missense variants; and mouse skeletal muscle appears less sensitive to D4Z4 chromatin modifiers than lymphoid tissue, which is where the DUX4 rise was seen. Read this as evidence about the model, not as evidence against a DNMT3B contribution in patients.

edges.description: The methylation half of the lesion does transfer: losing Dnmt3b demethylates the D4Z4 array in this mouse, and DUX4 rises, but in secondary lymphoid organs rather than muscle.
edges.limitations: Derepression is demonstrated in lymphoid tissue, not in the muscle compartment where FSHD manifests, so the node is reproduced in the wrong tissue.

edges.description: Produces a disturbed vascular phenotype from misexpression of a gene at the FSHD locus, offering a mechanism for a disease feature that the DUX4-in-skeletal-muscle account does not reach.
edges.limitations: Three gaps separate this from the human phenotype. The readouts are whole-embryo and tadpole vasculature, not retina, so the tissue in which patients present is not examined. The manipulation is systemic overexpression of frg1, whereas FRG1 is a candidate whose upregulation in patient muscle has been contested and which the field has largely displaced in favour of DUX4 — so the model may be modelling a gene that is not the effector. And the direction is inverted between arms: knockdown reduces angiogenesis while overexpression increases branching, so the model does not by itself say which dose change, if either, corresponds to the patient state.

nodes.description: The second locus, and the reason FSHD4 is digenic rather than dominant at one gene. Only a 4qA subtelomere carries the pLAM polyadenylation signal immediately distal to the last D4Z4 unit; on that background the distal DUX4 transcript is efficiently polyadenylated and stable enough to persist in somatic cells, whereas non-permissive 4qB and chromosome 10q backgrounds lack a usable signal. It is modelled separately from the derepressing lesion because the two segregate independently and disease needs both: a DNMT3B variant without a permissive allele derepresses an array whose transcript cannot be stabilised.

nodes.description: A telangiectatic, sometimes exudative retinal vasculopathy resembling Coats disease is the ophthalmologic extramuscular feature of FSHD. Like hearing loss, it clusters in early-onset disease with large D4Z4 deletions, and it is the human counterpart of the vascular arm of the disease that the frog FRG1 model addresses.

nodes.description: The only model to address why FSHD has an ophthalmologic component at all. frg1 is expressed in frog vasculature; knocking it down reduces angiogenesis and DAB2 expression, and overexpressing it produces excess vessel branching, vessel dilation and edema. Read carefully, this is a candidate-gene result from before the field settled on DUX4: it shows that a gene at the FSHD locus can produce a vascular phenotype when its dose is wrong, not that FRG1 dosage is what causes vasculopathy in patients.
